intents.title: Greeting
intents.answer: Hi! I'm CyberAware, your cybersecurity awareness assistant. Ask me about phishing, passwords, OTP scams, SIM swaps, POPIA and more, or try the phishing and password checkers.

intents.title: Thanks
intents.answer: You're welcome! Stay sharp out there. 🔐

intents.title: Goodbye
intents.answer: Goodbye! Remember: when in doubt, don't click, and never share your OTP.

intents.title: What can you do?
intents.answer:
I can explain common cyber threats and how to protect yourself. I also have three tools:

- **Phishing checker**: paste a suspicious SMS, email or WhatsApp message and I'll point out red flags.
- **Password checker**: estimates how strong a password is (nothing is stored).
- **Quiz**: test what you know.

Try asking: *"How do I spot a phishing email?"* or *"What is a SIM swap?"*

intents.title: Phishing emails
patterns: how do i spot a phishing email
email asking me to verify my account
email with a link to login
i clicked a link in a suspicious message
intents.answer:
**Phishing** is when criminals pretend to be a trusted organisation (a bank, SARS, a courier, your university) to trick you into clicking a link, opening an attachment or handing over details.

Common red flags:
- Urgency or threats: *"Your account will be suspended in 24 hours"*
- A generic greeting like *"Dear customer"*
- A sender address or link that doesn't match the real organisation's domain
- Requests for passwords, PINs, OTPs or card details
- Unexpected attachments or prizes
tips: Hover over links to see the real address before clicking.
Go to the organisation's website or app yourself instead of using the link.
Paste the message into the Phishing checker for a second opinion.
Clicked a link already? Don't enter any details. If you did, change that password straight away and contact the organisation.

intents.title: SMS and phone scams (smishing and vishing)
patterns: someone called me pretending to be the bank
intents.answer:
**Smishing** is phishing by SMS or WhatsApp, and **vishing** is phishing by voice call. Scammers often pose as your bank's fraud department, a courier with a "failed delivery", or a cellphone network offering an upgrade.

A real bank will never ask you to read out an OTP, PIN or password over the phone, or to move money to a "safe account".
tips: Hang up and call the number on the back of your card or on the official website.
Don't trust caller ID: numbers can be spoofed.
Never install an app or "remote support" tool because a caller asked you to.

intents.title: OTP scams
patterns: should i share my one time pin
can i give the bank my otp
they asked me to read the code sent to my phone
intents.answer:
A **one-time PIN (OTP)** is the final key that approves a payment, a new device or a password reset. Whoever has it can act as you.

**Never share an OTP with anyone**, including someone who says they're from your bank, a courier or a store. Legitimate organisations will never ask for it.

Always read the full OTP message: it usually says what it's approving (for example, a payment amount or a new device link).
tips: If you get an OTP you didn't request, someone may be trying to access your account. Contact your bank through official channels.
Treat OTPs like cash.

intents.title: SIM swap fraud
patterns: my phone suddenly has no signal
how to protect against sim swap
lost signal and got bank messages
intents.answer:
In **SIM swap fraud**, a criminal convinces or bribes someone at a cellphone network to move your number onto their SIM card. They then receive your OTPs and can take over your banking and other accounts.

Warning sign: your phone suddenly shows *No service* or *Emergency calls only* for no clear reason.
tips: If you lose signal unexpectedly, contact your network and your bank immediately.
Ask your network about extra SIM swap protection such as a PIN or in-store ID checks.
Use an authenticator app instead of SMS for 2FA where possible.

intents.title: Strong passwords
patterns: how do i create a strong password
how long should my password be
should i use the same password everywhere
intents.answer:
A strong password is **long, unique and unpredictable**.

- Use a **passphrase** of 4+ random words, e.g. `harbour-velvet-cactus-ninety` (don't use this one!).
- Aim for at least **12–15 characters**.
- **Never reuse** passwords: when one site is breached, attackers try the same login everywhere (*credential stuffing*).
- Avoid names, birthdays, sports teams and patterns like `Password123!`.
tips: Use a password manager so you only need to remember one strong master password.
Try the Password checker tab to see how a password holds up.

intents.title: Password managers
patterns: should i use a password manager
how do i remember all my passwords
where should i store my passwords
intents.answer:
A **password manager** generates and stores a unique, strong password for every account, so you only have to remember one master password.

Reputable managers encrypt your vault so that even the provider can't read it. That's far safer than reusing passwords, writing them in a notes app or keeping them in a spreadsheet.
tips: Protect the password manager itself with a strong master passphrase and 2FA.
Built-in browser and phone password managers are a good start if you use one device ecosystem.

intents.title: Multi-factor authentication (2FA/MFA)
intents.answer:
**Multi-factor authentication (MFA or 2FA)** means logging in needs something you *know* (a password) **plus** something you *have* (your phone or a security key) or *are* (a fingerprint).

Even if your password leaks, an attacker still can't get in without the second factor. Turn it on for email, banking, social media and cloud storage first.

Strongest to weakest: security keys and passkeys → authenticator apps → SMS codes (SMS is still much better than nothing).
tips: Save your backup or recovery codes somewhere safe.
Never approve a login prompt you didn't start (*MFA fatigue* attacks).

intents.title: Public Wi-Fi
patterns: can i do banking on public wifi
intents.answer:
Public Wi-Fi is convenient but risky. Attackers can set up fake hotspots with names like *"Mall Free WiFi"* to intercept traffic or show fake login pages.

Most sites use HTTPS today, which protects much of your traffic, but it's still wise to avoid sensitive tasks on open networks.
tips: Use mobile data or your own hotspot for banking.
Confirm the exact network name with staff.
Turn off auto-connect to open networks.
A reputable VPN adds a layer of protection on untrusted networks.

intents.title: Ransomware
patterns: hackers want payment to unlock files
intents.answer:
**Ransomware** is malware that encrypts your files or systems and demands payment, often in cryptocurrency, to unlock them. Many groups also steal data and threaten to leak it.

Paying is no guarantee you'll get your data back, and it funds further crime.
tips: Keep offline or versioned backups and test that you can restore them.
Keep your operating system and apps updated.
If infected, disconnect the device from the network and get professional help.

intents.title: Malware and suspicious attachments
intents.answer:
**Malware** is any software designed to harm you: viruses, trojans, spyware, keyloggers and ransomware. It often arrives through email attachments, fake software updates, cracked or pirated apps, and malicious ads.

Be especially careful with `.exe`, `.zip`, `.iso` and macro-enabled Office files (`.docm`, `.xlsm`) that you weren't expecting.
tips: Keep built-in protection (such as Microsoft Defender) switched on and updated.
Only install apps from official stores or vendor websites.
If you opened something suspicious, disconnect from the internet, run a full scan and change passwords from a different, clean device.

intents.title: Social engineering
patterns: someone pretending to be it support
intents.answer:
**Social engineering** targets people rather than technology. Attackers use **urgency, authority, fear, curiosity or helpfulness** to get you to bypass normal checks.

Examples: a fake "IT support" call asking for your password, someone following you through a secure door (*tailgating*), or a message from a "manager" asking for an urgent favour.
tips: Slow down: pressure is a red flag.
Verify requests through a separate, trusted channel.
It's okay to say no and check first.

intents.title: Software updates
patterns: why should i update my phone
intents.answer:
Updates fix **security vulnerabilities** that attackers actively exploit. An unpatched phone, browser or operating system is one of the easiest ways in.

Turn on automatic updates for your OS, browser and apps, and replace devices that no longer receive security updates.
tips: Restart when prompted: many updates only apply after a reboot.

intents.title: Backups
patterns: how should i back up my files
intents.answer:
Backups are your safety net against ransomware, theft and hardware failure. Follow the **3-2-1 rule**:

- **3** copies of your data
- on **2** different types of storage
- with **1** copy offsite or offline

Cloud services with version history count as an offsite copy.
tips: Test restoring a file now and then: a backup you can't restore isn't a backup.

intents.title: Social media privacy
patterns: what should i not post online
is it safe to post my location
intents.answer:
What you share publicly can be used for scams, identity theft and guessing security questions: your birthday, ID number, school, pet's name, home address or travel plans.

Review your privacy settings, limit who can see your posts, and think before posting real-time locations or photos of documents, tickets or boarding passes.
tips: Search your own name online to see what others can find.

intents.title: POPIA (South Africa)
patterns: company shared my data without consent
intents.answer:
The **Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA)** is South Africa's main data-protection law. It sets conditions for how organisations collect, use, store and share personal information, and requires them to keep it secure.

If an organisation suffers a security compromise involving personal information, it must notify the **Information Regulator** and the affected people as soon as reasonably possible.

If you believe your information was misused, you can complain to the organisation first and then to the Information Regulator.
tips: After a breach notice, change affected passwords and watch for targeted phishing.
This is general information, not legal advice.

intents.title: My account was hacked
patterns: what do i do if i get hacked
intents.answer:
Act quickly:

1. **Change the password** from a device you trust, and change it anywhere else you reused it.
2. **Turn on 2FA** and sign out of all other sessions.
3. **Check recovery settings**: attackers often change the recovery email or phone number.
4. **Review activity**: forwarding rules, sent messages, connected apps, payments.
5. **Warn your contacts** if messages were sent from your account.
6. Use the platform's official account-recovery process if you're locked out.
tips: If money or banking details are involved, contact your bank immediately.

intents.title: I've been scammed
patterns: i gave my banking details to a scammer
money was taken from my account
what do i do if i was defrauded
how to report a scam in south africa
intents.answer:
Time matters. Do these straight away:

1. **Call your bank** using the number on the back of your card or in the official app. Block cards and stop or dispute transactions.
2. **Change passwords and PINs** for banking and email.
3. **Report it to SAPS** and get a case number, which banks and insurers often need.
4. **Keep evidence**: screenshots, messages, phone numbers, transaction references.
5. **Watch for follow-up scams**, such as people offering to "recover" your money for a fee.
tips: Being scammed isn't a sign of stupidity: these criminals are professionals. Reporting helps protect others.

intents.title: Safe online shopping
patterns: too good to be true deal
intents.answer:
Fake stores and marketplace scams spike around sales like Black Friday.

Red flags:
- Prices that are far too low
- A newly created website, poor contact details, or only EFT or crypto accepted
- Sellers who pressure you to pay outside the platform
- Buyers who send a "proof of payment" (POP) and ask you to release goods: **POPs can be faked**, so wait until the money clears in your own account
tips: Use card payments or secure checkout services that offer buyer protection.

intents.title: QR code scams (quishing)
patterns: scanned a qr code on a poster
intents.answer:
**Quishing** uses QR codes to hide malicious links. Criminals stick fake QR codes over real ones on parking meters, posters and restaurant tables, or put them in emails to get past link filters.

After scanning, check the web address your phone shows **before** opening it, and never enter login or card details on a site you reached through an unexpected QR code.

intents.title: WhatsApp account takeover
patterns: someone asked for my whatsapp code
friend asked me to send a code by mistake
intents.answer:
A common scam: a "friend" (whose account is already hijacked) says they sent you a code by mistake and asks you to forward it. That code is **your** WhatsApp registration code, and sharing it hands over your account.

Protect yourself: in WhatsApp go to **Settings → Account → Two-step verification** and set a PIN.
tips: If a friend's message seems odd, call them on a different channel to check.

intents.title: Invoice and business email fraud
patterns: ceo asked me to make urgent payment
email asking to update banking details
my boss asked me to buy gift cards
manager emailed asking for an urgent favour
intents.answer:
In **business email compromise (BEC)**, criminals impersonate a supplier, landlord or executive (sometimes from a real, hacked mailbox) and ask for payment to "new" bank details.

Always **verify changes to banking details by phone**, using a number you already have rather than one in the email.

intents.title: AI, deepfake and investment scams
patterns: fake video of a celebrity investment
family member calling asking for money urgently
intents.answer:
AI tools can now clone voices from short clips and create convincing fake videos. Scammers use them for fake *"family emergency"* calls and for celebrity-endorsed investment adverts.

Agree on a **family safe word**, and verify urgent requests by calling the person back on a number you know.
tips: Be sceptical of investment adverts promising guaranteed high returns, whoever appears to endorse them.

intents.title: Lost or stolen phone
patterns: what to do if my laptop is stolen
intents.answer:
If your phone or laptop is lost or stolen:

1. Use **Find My (Apple) or Find My Device (Google)** to locate, lock or wipe it.
2. Ask your network to **block the SIM** so it can't receive your OTPs.
3. Tell your bank, and change key passwords from another device.
4. Report it to SAPS for a case number.

Prevention: use a strong screen lock, enable device encryption, and keep backups.

intents.title: Job and internship scams
patterns: they want me to pay for training before the job
too good to be true job
intents.answer:
Job scams target students and graduates. Warning signs:

- You're asked to **pay** for training, uniforms, a medical or a "placement fee"
- An interview held only over WhatsApp or Telegram
- An offer without a proper interview
- Requests for your ID, bank details or OTP before any contract exists

Legitimate employers don't charge you to work for them.
tips: Check the vacancy on the company's official careers page.
